newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists rebuff Juppe on electoral reform.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists rebuff Juppe on electoral reform.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist party has rebuffed a request from Prime Minister Alain Juppe for proposals for electoral reform.

Juppe wrote to the leaders of all parliamentary parties this week asking their views on the voting system, the place of women and young people in politics, age limits for office-holders and a limit on the number of offices a politician may hold at once.
In a reply released on Wednesday, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin mailed Juppe his party's published proposals for limiting office-holding and increasing women's political role.

"On changing the voting system -- if that is your intention -- I do not believe this question is at the heart of the French people's expectations today, since they are much more concerned with economic difficulties and rising unemployment," he wrote.
The prime minister suggested last month adding a "dose" of proportional representation to the majority voting system for parliamentary elections, meeting opposition in his centre-right coalition.

Liberation said that in his letter, Juppe also raised the idea of barring triangular run-offs in parliamentary elections by limiting the second round to the top two candidates, where no one wins an outright majority on the first ballot.
That would hit the extreme-right National Front, which has vowed to keep its candidates in the race wherever it receives more than the required 12.5 percent of registered voters.

He also proposed changing the voting system for regional elections from the present proportional representation, which gives the National Front the balance of power in some areas, to a method which gives the biggest party a premium.
Jospin complained at being sent a multiple-choice questionnaire by Juppe.

"May I hope you share my view that asking us to fill in a questionnaire is neither a normal nor a fortunate formula for conducting relations between the prime minister and political leaders, especially with the opposition," he said.

Jospin noted that he had made modernising France's political institutions a major plank of his presidential election campaign 18 months ago, suggesting the president's term of office be cut to five years from seven.
Conservative Gaullist President Jacques Chirac, who defeated Jospin, said at the time that constitutional reform was not the issue of the moment.
